opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the central tensions of the whole project. When you open participation to the world, contributions don't arrive evenly. Some languages have large, very active communities that show up early and contribute a lot. Others, often the ones we most want to serve because they've been neglected, may have only a handful of contributors. So we expect, and we're already seeing, a long tail: a few languages with a lot of data and many with very little.

I think about it at a few levels. The first is to be honest that imbalance is the default state of the world, not a bug in our process. Most of the internet is in a small number of languages, and that's why existing models do poorly on everything else. Aya is partly a reaction to that, so we can't just passively accept whatever distribution we get. We have to actively counterbalance it.

In practice that means a few things. On the community side, we invest in outreach for underrepresented languages: language ambassadors, local leads, making the contribution platform easy to use, and celebrating contributors so there's a sense of ownership. A lot of the work is human and organizational, not technical.

On the data side, we also lean on approaches beyond pure human annotation. Translation of high-quality datasets and templating existing resources can raise the floor for low-resource languages. But we're careful about that, because translated data carries artifacts, so-called "translationese," and can miss cultural nuance. So we treat human-written, culturally grounded data as especially precious and try not to let it be swamped by synthetic or translated data.

Then on the modeling side, there are well-known levers: how you sample across languages during training, upsampling low-resource languages without overfitting to the few examples you have, and thinking about how much capacity each language gets. There's a real trade-off. If you push too hard toward balance you can hurt performance on high-resource languages, and if you don't push at all, the long tail gets ignored. Part of the research contribution is understanding that trade-off rather than pretending it doesn't exist.

The last piece is evaluation. If you only measure aggregate performance, the imbalance hides inside the average. So we want to report per-language results, be transparent about where the model is weak, and release the data so others can see exactly what the distribution looks like. I'd rather people know precisely where coverage is thin than claim we've "solved" multilinguality. Imbalance is something you manage and are transparent about, not something you fully eliminate.

r001.rationale: The response says contributions do not arrive evenly: active communities contribute a lot, while other languages may have only a handful of contributors. This directly links dataset skew to who participates.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, and honestly it's one of the most interesting parts of the project. The reality is that imbalance is baked in from the start. If you look at where the internet's text comes from, or where the people with time and access to contribute are, you end up with a very skewed picture. Some languages, like English, Spanish, maybe Hindi or Arabic, have large communities and tons of existing data. And then you have languages where there may be millions of speakers but almost no digital footprint, and only a handful of people who even know the project exists.

So I'd say we think about it on a few levels. The first is just being honest that we are not going to get a perfectly balanced dataset. That was never a realistic goal. What we care about more is coverage, meaning can we get meaningful, high-quality examples for as many languages as possible, even if the counts differ by an order of magnitude or more. For a lot of these languages, going from zero instruction data to a few thousand curated examples is a massive step, and it changes what's possible for modeling.

The second is that we try to distinguish between quantity and quality. For low-resource languages, the data we get from native speakers who are annotating and editing is often much more valuable per example than large volumes of machine-translated or scraped text, because those automatic pipelines tend to be worst exactly in the languages that need help the most. So part of the design of Aya was to get humans in the loop in a way that gives us signal where the automated signals are weakest.

And then the third piece is on the modeling side. Imbalance in the data doesn't have to translate one-to-one into imbalance in the model. There's a lot you can do with how you sample, how you weight languages during training, how you think about transfer between related languages. So we see the dataset as one input, and the research question is really how you combine that with sampling strategies and architecture choices so the long tail actually benefits.

The last thing I'd say is that it's also a community question, not just a technical one. A lot of the imbalance reflects who has been invited to participate in building these systems historically. So part of what we're trying to do with Aya is widen that, bring in people from language communities that have been left out, and treat them as collaborators rather than just data sources. That doesn't fix the imbalance overnight, but it changes the trajectory.

r001.rationale: The response says the skew reflects which people have time and access to contribute, and later connects imbalance to who has historically been invited to participate.

astra-6.text:
I think imbalance is inevitable when you’re working across languages, but that doesn’t mean we should accept it as a given. One of the challenges is that if you simply pool all the data together, the languages with the most data can dominate. You can end up with a multilingual model that works very well for a handful of languages and much less well for the rest.

So I think about both the data we collect and how we use it. Where do we need to invest in getting more contributions? How do we sample during training so that smaller language communities have a meaningful influence on the model? And then, how do we evaluate each language, rather than letting a single average hide those differences?

There’s also a quality dimension. The number of examples doesn’t tell you whether they reflect the ways people actually use a language, or the cultural contexts that matter to them. That’s why community participation is so important. The goal isn’t just to have a language represented in the dataset; it’s to make something useful for the people who speak it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uneven data volumes and the need for more contributions and community participation, but it does not clearly explain that the dataset’s skew reflects who participates in the project.

sol-6.1.text:
I think imbalance is inevitable when you’re working across languages, because the starting point is already so unequal. For some languages, there’s a huge amount of digitized text, and for others, very little. So if we simply let the available data dictate the composition of the dataset, we reproduce those inequalities.

With Aya, part of the opportunity is to be more deliberate about whose contributions we’re bringing in and which languages need more support. But it’s not just a question of getting the same number of examples for every language. You also care about quality, diversity, and whether those examples reflect how people actually use the language.

And then you have to evaluate at the language level. An aggregate improvement can hide the fact that some languages aren’t benefiting at all. So I think of this as an ongoing process: understand the gaps, target the data collection, and check whether the resulting model is actually improving for those communities.

r001.rationale: The response says Aya can deliberately choose whose contributions to include, but attributes dataset imbalance to unequal amounts of digitized text. It does not clearly state that dataset skew reflects who participates in the project.
